# II. The Controller Cases

In Kahn v. Lynch Communication Systems, the controller held 43.3% of the shares and threatened a hostile tender offer if the special committee did not accept its price.[^1] The court held that the committee's approval shifted the burden only if the committee had real bargaining power, and it found that the threat had stripped the committee of it.

In Kahn v. Tremont Corp., the controller dominated a three-member committee whose members had business ties to it.[^2] The court held that the committee had not functioned independently, so the burden stayed with the defendants, and it remanded for a fairness determination.

In Kahn v. M & F Worldwide Corp., the controller conditioned its offer from the outset on approval by an independent committee and a majority of the minority.[^3] The court held that business-judgment review applied because both conditions were in place before negotiations began.

[^1]: Kahn v. Lynch Commc'n Sys., Inc., 638 A.2d 1110, 1117 (Del. 1994).
[^2]: Kahn v. Tremont Corp., 694 A.2d 422, 429 (Del. 1997).
[^3]: Kahn v. M & F Worldwide Corp., 88 A.3d 635, 644 (Del. 2014).
